papers.title: Mitophagy in neurodegeneration: crosstalk between PRKN/parkin-dependent and PRKN-independent pathways.
papers.summary: Mitophagy is the process by which damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared from cells, and this paper reviews how this process is disrupted in neurodegenerative diseases. It focuses on two main molecular routes: one dependent on the protein PRKN/parkin (linked to Parkinson's disease) and other pathways that work independently of PRKN. The review discusses how these two routes interact and overlap, highlighting shared regulators and points of crosstalk that could be relevant to disease progression.
papers.why: Understanding both PRKN-dependent and PRKN-independent mitophagy pathways is essential for interpreting how mitochondrial quality control fails in neurons, providing mechanistic context for the PhD project's focus on mitophagy dysregulation in neurodegeneration.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram illustrating the molecular crosstalk and convergence points between PRKN-dependent and PRKN-independent mitophagy pathways.

papers.title: Metformin Ameliorates Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction via p53/Parkin-Mediated Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the diabetes drug metformin affects cognitive decline associated with diabetes. The researchers found that metformin improves cognitive function by promoting mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, through a p53/Parkin signaling pathway. This suggests that enhancing mitochondrial quality control in neurons could be a therapeutic strategy for diabetes-related cognitive impairment.
papers.why: This paper provides direct mechanistic evidence linking a specific molecular pathway (p53/Parkin-mediated mitophagy) to neuronal health and cognitive outcomes, relevant to the mitophagy focus of the PhD project even though it lacks spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics or interneuron-specific data.

papers.title: Exercise alleviates neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aged mice via hepatic FGF21-driven microglial mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study shows that exercise in aged mice triggers a liver-brain signaling pathway where the hormone FGF21 is released and travels to the brain. There, FGF21 promotes mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria) in microglia, the brain's immune cells. This reduces neuroinflammation and improves cognitive function in the aged mice.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates a systemic hepatic-to-brain axis regulating microglial mitophagy and neuroinflammation, offering mechanistic and methodological parallels for studying mitophagy regulation in neurons and its links to brain aging.

papers.title: Naringin reduces mitochondrial fragmentation and excessive mitophagy in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury via the S-nitrosylated Dynamin-related protein 1 (SNO-DRP1) / Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) / Mitochondrial Calcium Uniporter (MCU) pathway.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how naringin, a natural flavonoid compound, protects brain cells during ischemia-reperfusion injury (damage that occurs when blood flow is restored after a stroke). The researchers found that naringin works by reducing a specific chemical modification of a mitochondrial fission protein called DRP1, which in turn affects a signaling pathway involving LRRK2 and MCU proteins. This intervention helps prevent mitochondria from fragmenting excessively and being degraded too much through mitophagy, ultimately protecting brain cells from damage.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it details molecular mechanisms of mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial fragmentation in neurons, directly connecting to the core mitochondrial quality control pathways central to the PhD project's focus.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitochondrial morphology (fragmented vs. intact networks) alongside mitophagy markers and DRP1 S-nitrosylation levels across treatment groups would be most informative for understanding the pathway mechanism.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture mitigates cognitive impairment caused by CPB by facilitating PINK1-dependent mitophagy and synaptic plasticity.
papers.summary: This study investigates whether electroacupuncture can improve cognitive problems caused by cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) surgery. The researchers focus on a mitophagy pathway involving the protein PINK1, which helps clear damaged mitochondria from cells. They also examine synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or reorganize neural connections, as a mechanism behind the cognitive benefits observed.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly examines PINK1-dependent mitophagy in neurons and its link to synaptic plasticity, connecting core mitophagy mechanisms to functional cognitive outcomes in the brain.

papers.title: Autophagy-Related Gene-Set Signals in the Genetic Architecture of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Hypothesis-Generating Link to Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide-Associated Cellular Maintenance Biology.
papers.summary: This study looks at whether genetic variants in autophagy-related genes are statistically overrepresented in genome-wide data for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The authors report a hypothesis-generating association between autophagy gene-sets and OCD genetic architecture, and further link this to NAD-associated cellular maintenance pathways. The work is exploratory, suggesting autophagy and NAD biology as candidate mechanisms worth further investigation in OCD, rather than providing direct mechanistic or experimental proof.
papers.why: This paper is tangential but potentially useful background since it highlights genetic evidence connecting autophagy machinery to neuropsychiatric disease, which could inform hypotheses about autophagy/mitophagy dysregulation in specific neuronal populations like interneurons in your project.

papers.title: Interplay between RNA m<sup>6</sup>A modification and transglutaminase 2 inhibitor effects on mitophagy dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how RNA m6A methylation, an epigenetic modification affecting mRNA stability and translation, interacts with transglutaminase 2 (TG2) inhibitors to influence mitophagy dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease. The study likely explores whether blocking TG2 activity can restore proper clearance of damaged mitochondria, a process known to be impaired in neurodegenerative disease. The abstract suggests a mechanistic link between RNA modification pathways and mitochondrial quality control that could reveal new therapeutic targets for AD.
papers.why: This work connects directly to the mitophagy dysfunction component of the profile's core research focus, offering molecular mechanisms relevant to neuronal health in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Activation of mitophagy by lidocaine limits mROS and prevents microglial M1 polarization to alleviate postoperative delirium.
papers.summary: This paper studies postoperative delirium, a cognitive disturbance following surgery, and finds that lidocaine can help prevent it. The mechanism involves lidocaine activating mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria), which reduces mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS). This reduction in mROS prevents microglia from switching to their pro-inflammatory M1 state, thereby alleviating delirium symptoms.
papers.why: This paper's focus on mitophagy activation and mitochondrial ROS regulation in the brain directly relates to the mitophagy mechanisms central to the PhD project, even though the disease context (delirium/microglia) differs from the neuronal/interneuron focus.
